James Fraser of Brea
jaymz FRAY-zer of bray
proper noun
From the Scots surname Fraser, of Norman origin; with the place-name Brea in Ross-shire; James from the Hebrew Ya’aqov, “Jacob, supplanter.”

📖 Biblical Definition

James Fraser of Brea (1639–1699) was a Covenanter minister whose Memoirs stand among the choicest records of a soul’s dealings with God in the seventeenth-century Kirk. Born to a Highland estate, he was brought through deep and prolonged spiritual conflict, wrestling long under conviction and the temptations of unbelief before he came to a settled rest in the free grace of Christ, and he set down these inward exercises with a searching honesty that has made his Memoirs a mirror for the exercised believer. Called to preach in the days of persecution, he laboured as an outed minister among the scattered flock, was seized for holding conventicles, and suffered long imprisonment upon the Bass Rock and in Blackness for the crown rights of Christ. His writings trace the LORD’s patient dealings in the conversion and establishing of a soul, the darkness before the dawn of assurance, and the sovereignty of grace that will not let the elect go. His life preaches that God often brings His people to Himself through long and painful travail, that the record of a soul’s dealings with the LORD may strengthen many after, and that imprisonment for the gospel is no loss to the man whose treasure is in Christ. He counted his inward history worth the writing, that others might see the same grace at work in themselves.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Covenanter minister and prisoner whose Memoirs record a soul’s deep dealings with God.

James Fraser of Brea (1639–1699), Scottish Covenanter minister of Highland birth.

Brought to Christ through long and searching spiritual conflict under conviction of sin.

Author of the Memoirs, a treasured record of a soul’s inward dealings with God.

Laboured as an outed minister and was imprisoned on the Bass Rock and at Blackness.

His writings trace the sovereignty of grace through darkness to settled assurance.

Psa 40:2 — "He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings."

Psa 34:19 — "Many are the afflictions of the righteous: but the LORD delivereth him out of them all."

Rom 8:38 — "For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come,"

Psa 66:16 — "Come and hear, all ye that fear God, and I will declare what he hath done for my soul."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the honest record of God’s dealings with the soul.

expand to see more

James Fraser of Brea is preserved because his Memoirs lay bare the LORD’s patient and sovereign dealings in the making of a Christian, the long conflict, the temptations to unbelief, and the settled rest at last in free grace. His searching honesty rebukes an age of shallow testimony that knows nothing of travail of soul and would have assurance without the LORD’s deep work.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from Fraser is that God frequently brings His people to Himself through long and painful exercise, and that the honest record of His dealings with a soul may declare to others what He has done, strengthening those who walk the same dark valley. His experience magnifies the sovereignty of grace that will not let the elect go, and his imprisonment for the gospel witnesses that no bond can rob the believer of a treasure hid in Christ.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name is joined to the Puritan and Covenanter tradition of recording God’s sovereign dealings with the soul.

expand to see more

Fraser’s Memoirs root the practice of tracing God’s patient work in the conversion of a soul.

His long conflict shows that assurance is often the fruit of deep and prolonged travail.

His experience magnifies the sovereignty of grace that keeps and establishes the elect.

His imprisonment on the Bass Rock joins him to the suffering remnant of the Covenant.

His honest testimony obeys the call to declare what the LORD has done for the soul.

Usage

"His long spiritual conflict is invoked to comfort those brought slowly to assurance."

"His imprisonment on the Bass Rock is remembered among the sufferings of the Covenanters."
